Le vendredi 25 septembre 2015 12:36:12 UTC+2, Susanne Flach a écrit :
> Assuming you don't need the list for other purposes, you could also read your data in as a data frame directly:
>
> test.file <- read.delim(choose.file(), sep=" ")
>
> read.delim takes a delimited table (here: whitespace), with one case per line, and interprets the first line as a header (as header=T is the default). This assumes that all lines (i.e. all your entries) have an equal number of column values, but all other solutions suggested so far would assume that, too.
>
> Then proceed from there (like creating dataframes with certain columns, saving back to file etc.)
>
> Am Donnerstag, 24. September 2015 21:36:39 UTC+2 schrieb Christophe Bechet:
> > Just one thing: in using write.csv, the output in my spreadsheet is only one column grouping everything separated by a comma. So, instead of write.csv, I used write.table, which gave me the desired output. For every soul interested in what was aiming at, I paste the lines of code here.
> >
> > # 1) Create a list with a few examples from the text file
> >
> > token.lemma.pos.grouping<-list(c("@", "@", "@", "_o:I222p30601.SBH06", "Markup(samp)", "-" , "-", "-"), c("Wj",  "wj",  "wj",  "wij" ,"404", "-" ,  "-" ,  "-"  ))
> >
> > # 2) Convert the list into a data frame so that each vector of the list gets its own row
> >
> > token.lemma.pos.1<- data.frame(matrix(unlist(token.lemma.pos.grouping), nrow=length(token.lemma.pos.grouping), byrow=T), stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
> >
> > # 3) Reduce the columns to those containing token, lemma and pos only
> >
> > token.lemma.pos.2<-token.lemma.pos.1[,c(1, 4, 5)]
> >
> > # 4) Save the output to a file. If necessary, rename each column header
> >
> > write.table(token.lemma.pos.2, file=choose.files(), sep="\t", quote=F, col.names=c("TOKEN", "LEMMA", "POS"), row.names=F)

> > > > > I'm trying to convert a lemmatized corpus into a data frame. In the corpus, every line shows instances of a spelling variant and its lemmas. Each line counts 8 words. It looks more like a dictionary without POS tags.
> > > > >
> > > > > First, in order for each word in each line to appear in a separate column, I needed to split the file at every space:
> > > > >
> > > > > > text.file<-scan(file=choose.files(), what="char", sep="\n", quiet=T)
> > > > > > text.file.2<-strsplit(text.file, " ")

> > > > > [1] "@"                   "@"                   "@"                   "_o:I222p30601.SBH06"

> > > > >

> > > > > [[3]]
> > > > > [1] "scepenne_" "scepenne_" "scepennen" "schepen"   "014"       "-"         "-"         "-"

messages.subject: Re: [CorpLing with R] Concordance of potential Dutch Verb-particle Constructions in big corpora

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm currently trying to make a concordance of potential Dutch compound verbs in a POS tagged corpus. The corpus is 100 files big and it amounts to 17,254,537 tokens, which is very big indeed.

Here I give a sample from that corpus:

# every token is assigned a POS tag and a lemma: token<POS><lemma>

corpus.file <- "Niet<adv><niet> lang<adj><lang> daarna<pronadv><daarna> kwam<verbpastsg><komen> er<pronadv><er> in<prep><in> zijne<det__poss><zijn> plaats<nounsg><plaats> een<det__art><een> heer<nounsg><heer> binnen<prep><binnen> van<prep><van> een<det__art><een> zeven-<num_card><zeven> of<conjcoord><of> achtentwintig<num_card><achtentwintig> jaren<nounpl><jaar>,<punc><,> naar<prep><naar> ik<pronpers><ik> berekende<verbpapa><berekenen>.<$.><.>"

Now, I give the code to make the concordance of a potential compound verb, using exact.matches:

source("C:/_qclwr/_scripts/_scripts_code-exerciseboxes_chapters_3-5/exact_matches_new.R")

all.matches.compverb<-vector()

for(i in corpus.file) {

  current.corpus.file<-scan(i, what="char", sep="\n", quiet=T)
  current.matches.compverb<-exact.matches("<verb.{3,6}><komen> (<([^verb.{3,6}]|[^[[:punct:]]])>[^<]*?){0,5}<prep|adv><
binnen>", current.corpus.file, case.sens=F, pcre=T)
  if(length(current.matches.compverb)==0) { next }
  all.matches.compverb<-append(all.matches.compverb, current.matches.compverb)
}

Expectedly, there is not enough space to handle this:

Error: cannot allocate vector of size 4.3 Mb
In addition: Warning messages:
1: In substr(lines, if (characters.around != 0) starts - characters.around else 1, : Reached total allocation of 3976Mb: see help(memory.size)
2: In substr(lines, if (characters.around != 0) starts - characters.around else 1, : Reached total allocation of 3976Mb: see help(memory.size)
3: In substr(lines, if (characters.around != 0) starts - characters.around else 1, : Reached total allocation of 3976Mb: see help(memory.size)
4: In substr(lines, if (characters.around != 0) starts - characters.around else 1, : Reached total allocation of 3976Mb: see help(memory.size)

I've tried to do this file by file, without success. I even tried the following to avoid the loop, once again without success:

whole.text <- unlist(lapply(corpus.file, function(x) scan(x, what="char", sep="\n", quiet=T))) # reads the content of the files in the vector
current.matches.compverb<-exact.matches("<verb.{3,6}><komen> (<([^verb.{3,6}]|[^[[:punct:]]]>[^<]*?){0,5}<prep|adv><binnen>", whole.text, case.sens=F, pcre=T)
all.matches.compverb<-append(all.matches.compverb, current.matches.compverb)

Any idea how I could achieve this without coming up against this problem of space?

Best regards and many thanks,

C. Bechet

messages.body_plain:
While I'm not sure about the space problem, a problem (or possibly, the problem) might be with the regex.

You likely need negative look-ahead "(?!...)" rather than "[^...]" to specify that "<komen>" should not be followed by a verb, nor by punctuation. The syntax "[^...]" only works for single characters, as "[...]" specifies a character class.

I got your sample to work by creating the following gnarly regex:

source("http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/exact_matches.r")

corpus.file <- "Niet<adv><niet> lang<adj><lang> daarna<pronadv><daarna> kwam<verbpastsg><komen> er<pronadv><er> in<prep><in> zijne<det__poss><zijn> plaats<nounsg><plaats> een<det__art><een> heer<nounsg><heer> binnen<prep><binnen> van<prep><van> een<det__art><een> zeven-<num_card><zeven> of<conjcoord><of> achtentwintig<num_card><achtentwintig> jaren<nounpl><jaar>,<punc><,> naar<prep><naar> ik<pronpers><ik> berekende<verbpapa><berekenen>.<$.><.>"

# gnarly regex
search.string <- "[^<>]+<verb[^>]{3,6}><komen>( [^<]+<((?!verb[^>]{3,6})[^>]*|(?![\\!\"\\#\\$\\%\\&\'\\(\\)\\*\\+\\,\\-\\.\\/\\:\\;\\<\\=\\>\\?\\@\\[\\\\\\]\\^\\_\\`\\{\\|\\}\\~]))><[^>]*>){0,6}[^<]+<(prep|adv)><binnen>"

exact.matches(search.string, corpus.file, case.sens = F, pcre = T)[[4]]

Here's the output, with tabs around "kwam<verbpastsg><komen> ... binnen<prep><binnen>":

[1] "Niet<adv><niet> lang<adj><lang> daarna<pronadv><daarna>\tkwam<verbpastsg><komen> er<pronadv><er> in<prep><in> zijne<det__poss><zijn> plaats<nounsg><plaats> een<det__art><een> heer<nounsg><heer> binnen<prep><binnen>\tvan<prep><van> een<det__art><een> zeven-<num_card><zeven> of<conjcoord><of> achtentwintig<num_card><achtentwintig> jaren<nounpl><jaar>,<punc><,> naar<prep><naar> ik<pronpers><ik> berekende<verbpapa><berekenen>.<$.><.>"
